title: Inattentional Blindness
summary: A demanding counting task on a dense static display that also contains a large object nobody was asked about. The learner commits to the count, submits it, answers a recognition question, and only then sees the same display again with everything labelled. Four deterministic variants let a lecturer repeat the demonstration with a different design rather than re-testing the same people, and a demonstrator route reveals the whole thing without spending a variant.
learningObjectives: Distinguish attention from awareness, and report from experience.
Explain why failing to report an unexpected object is not evidence that it was invisible.
Name the design factors that raise and lower noticing rates.
Explain why a single trial cannot measure anybody's attention.
Recognise that a retrospective recognition question is partly a memory test and partly a prompt.
interactionTypes: performed counting task on a static display
transparent replay with the object marked
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; the count and the recognition answer stay in the browser tab, nothing is written to storage, and the record of which variants have been used is a JavaScript variable that disappears on reload.
accessibilityNotes: The display is entirely static: nothing moves, nothing flashes, and there is no flicker of any rate, so the demonstration carries no photosensitivity risk and there is no motion for a reduced-motion rule to reduce. The only timed behaviour is an optional 25-second display limit, presented as a checkbox that can be switched off before a run starts, and the tool says plainly that switching it off makes the run fully self-paced. Shape and fill carry the task; no colour carries meaning anywhere. The live display is aria-hidden because a spoken inventory would answer the question being asked, and the reveal afterwards restates the entire display in words - every shape type and count, the object's grid position, and its size relative to the small shapes. Every control has an accessible name; the count field is a labelled number input; the recognition question is a radio group with a visible legend. Headings do not skip; focus moves to the reveal heading. Usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths with no horizontal page scroll.
readmeTopic: Inattentional blindness: attention, awareness, and a surprise that works exactly once
simulationNotes: Displays are generated deterministically from a fixed seed per variant (20260901 to 20260904) on a 12 by 7 grid with per-item jitter, so a variant is byte-identical every time it is drawn and a whole room can be given the same one. The unexpected object is placed first, never in the middle columns or the middle row, and the cells it would overlap are then kept empty, so a solid star can never hide a countable shape. The counted type is forced to between 6 and 10 instances, so the range stated on the page is always true. Variant A: 48 items, count solid downward triangles, correct count 9, large outlined star. Variant B: 72 items, same count, correct count 9, medium outlined star. Variant C: 48 items, count outlined squares, correct count 6, large outlined star that now shares its fill with the counted set. Variant D: 30 items, count solid downward triangles, correct count 6, large solid star. NO NOTICING RATES ARE REPORTED ANYWHERE. The tool has no data on how often people miss these objects, and an invented percentage would be worse than none; the variant table therefore reports what each variant changes rather than what it produces. Nothing here measures the user: one trial, one binary answer, no reliability and no norms, and the page says so in the reveal and again in the debrief.
